seo.title: Education — Venom Guitars
seo.description: Learn lutherie, guitar setup, tonewoods, electronics and more from Venom Guitars. Free guides and resources for players and builders.

s3.k1: From player to builder — knowledge is free
s3.k2: Whether you're setting up your first guitar or routing your first body blank, we share everything we know. Free guides, glossaries, FAQs, and deep dives into the craft of lutherie.

s4.k5: Why does the timber matter? We break down the acoustic and electrical properties of common guitar woods — Mahogany, Alder, Ash, Blackwood, Maple — and what they actually do to your tone.
s4.k9: A properly set up guitar plays itself. Learn how to adjust action, intonation, truss rod, and nut slots. This is the single most impactful skill any guitarist can learn.
s4.k13: Single coils, humbuckers, series/parallel, coil splits — we decode pickup wiring with clear diagrams. Includes common mods and how to shield your cavities properly.
s4.k17: Our signature technique. How we design, pour, and finish resin art guitar bodies. Covers pigment selection, mold prep, curing, sanding back, and applying a gloss topcoat.
s4.k21: Template making, router bit selection, climb cuts, and avoiding tear-out. We walk through routing a full guitar body — pickup cavities, neck pocket, control cavity, and contours.
s4.k25: The dark art of a proper fret job. We cover leveling beams, crowning files, micro-mesh polishing, and how to diagnose fret buzz vs nut or saddle issues. Includes video references.
s4.k29: A deep dive into native Australian timbers and their guitar-building properties. Blackwood, Silky Oak, Queensland Maple, Camphor Laurel, Huon Pine — their tone, workability, and availability.
s4.k33: Quartersawn vs flatsawn blanks, truss rod channels, headstock angles, fingerboard radius, and binding. A complete walkthrough of building a bolt-on guitar neck.
s4.k37: The never-ending debate — nitrocellulose vs polyester/polyurethane. We give you the actual facts on tone, durability, application, and why the answer depends entirely on your build.

s5.k3: One-page references you can print and pin above your workbench.
s5.k5: Standard action heights for Fender-style, Gibson-style, and acoustic guitars
s5.k7: How to measure neck relief and when (and when not) to adjust the truss rod
s5.k9: Getting your guitar to play in tune all the way up the neck
s5.k11: Recommended starting heights for single coils, P90s, and humbuckers
s5.k13: SSS, HSS, HH, HHH — common wiring configurations with mods
s5.k15: Side-by-side tone, weight, and workability ratings for 20+ tonewoods

s6.k3: Custom builds typically take 8–16 weeks depending on complexity. Resin art finishes, binding, and unique inlay work add time. We'll give you a realistic estimate when you enquire, and we'll keep you updated with photos throughout the process. We don't rush builds — every day spent is a better guitar.
s6.k4: We primarily use Australian hardwoods — Blackwood, Queensland Maple, Silky Oak, and Camphor Laurel — because we believe Australia has extraordinary tonewoods that deserve recognition. We also use international classics like Mahogany, Alder, and Ash when the build calls for it. All timber is responsibly sourced.
s6.k5: Absolutely. If you want Lollar pickups, Gotoh hardware, or a specific aged nickel bridge, we'll source it or you can supply it. We have preferred suppliers we recommend, but we're not locked in to any brand. Your build, your specs.
s6.k6: Yes to both. We ship Australia-wide and can arrange international shipping. Guitars are packed in hard cases with extensive protective packaging. International orders require additional time and cost — contact us for a shipping quote to your location.
s6.k7: A resin art finish means the body itself is partially or fully made from clear/pigmented epoxy resin, often combined with timber. It creates a completely unique visual — swirls, cells, layers of colour — that can never be exactly replicated. It's heavier than a solid wood body and requires more build time, but the visual result is genuinely one-of-a-kind.
s6.k8: By appointment, yes. We love having players and builders come through — it's a great way to discuss your build in person and see the timbers we have on hand. Reach out via the contact page and we'll arrange a time.
s6.k9: On a case-by-case basis. We primarily focus on new builds, but if you've got a guitar that needs serious work — a refret, nut replacement, or electronics overhaul — reach out and we'll let you know if we can fit it in.

s7.k3: Don't know your nut from your saddle? Your truss rod from your trust fund? We've got you.
s7.k5: The height of the strings above the frets. Low action = easier to play; too low = fret buzz. The goal is finding the sweet spot.
s7.k7: A strip of material (plastic, wood, or purfling) inlaid along the edge of the body, neck, or headstock. Decorative and protective.
s7.k9: A neck joint where the neck is bolted (or screwed) to the body. Used in Fender-style builds. Easier to replace than set or through-neck joints.
s7.k11: A mod that bypasses one coil of a humbucker, giving you a single-coil sound. Adds versatility; sound is thinner than a true single coil.
s7.k13: The process of levelling, re-crowning, and polishing frets to eliminate buzzing and inconsistencies. One of the highest-value guitar tech jobs.
s7.k15: A dual-coil pickup that cancels electromagnetic hum. Warmer, louder, and thicker-sounding than single coils. Used in Gibson-style guitars.
s7.k17: How accurately a guitar plays in tune up the neck. Set by adjusting saddle position so the 12th fret harmonic matches the fretted note.
s7.k19: A craftsperson who builds and/or repairs stringed instruments. The word comes from the French word for lute. We're electric luthiers.
s7.k21: The slotted piece at the top of the neck (between headstock and fretboard) that guides and spaces the strings. Material affects open-string tone and tuning stability.
s7.k23: Timber cut so the growth rings run roughly perpendicular to the face. More stable, resists warping, and shows beautiful medullary ray figure in species like Oak.
s7.k25: The slight forward bow in a guitar neck, controlled by the truss rod. A small amount of relief (0.1–0.3mm) is usually desirable for playability.
s7.k27: The vibrating string length from nut to saddle. Fender-style = 648mm (25.5"). Gibson-style = 628mm (24.75"). Affects tension, feel, and tone.
s7.k29: A steel rod running inside the neck that counteracts string tension. Adjusting it controls neck relief. Turn carefully and never force it.
s7.k31: Any timber used in instrument construction chosen for its acoustic properties. In electric guitars, the effect is subtle but real — body resonance affects sustain and character.
s7.k33: A fret installed at the nut position so open strings have the same tone as fretted notes. Used on some vintage and custom builds for consistent timbre.
s7.k37: Can't find the answer? Drop us a message and we'll either answer directly or turn it into a new guide.
